answer.policy_title: Surgery of the Shoulder – Commercial and Individual Exchange Medical Policy
criteria_quotes: Surgery of the shoulder is proven and medically necessary in certain circumstances. For medical necessity clinical coverage criteria, refer to the: ... InterQual® CP: Procedures: ... Joint Replacement, Shoulder
The InterQual® criteria are proprietary to Optum and are not published on this website.
answer.submission_route: Written appeals can be sent by mail to: UnitedHealthcare Member Inquiry/Appeals, P.O. Box 31393, Salt Lake City, UT 84131, or UnitedHealthCare Member Inquiry/Appeals, P.O. Box 740816, Atlanta, GA 30374-0816. Members may also submit appeals online through the member portal at myuhc.com.
answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: Because the governing InterQual criteria ('Joint Replacement, Shoulder') are proprietary to Optum, they are not fully disclosed in the public policy document. The patient can obtain a free, complete copy of the specific clinical criteria applied to their case by calling the UnitedHealthcare Customer Service number on the back of their member ID card or submitting a request in writing. Providers can access a read-only version of the InterQual criteria online by logging into the UnitedHealthcare Provider Portal (uhcprovider.com) with their One Healthcare ID and navigating to 'Policies' > 'Clinical Guidelines' > 'InterQual'.
answer.notes: The policy governing CPT code 23472 is 'Surgery of the Shoulder'. This policy defers the clinical medical-necessity criteria to InterQual's 'Joint Replacement, Shoulder' subset, which is proprietary and requires a portal login to view.

NOTICE OF ADVERSE BENEFIT DETERMINATION

Date of notice: 2026-08-04
Member: Emerson Brooks
Member ID: W628799962
Plan: UnitedHealthcare (Commercial/ACA), state of Iowa

Dear Emerson,

We reviewed the prior authorization request submitted by your provider for the following service:

    Requested service: Total shoulder replacement
    Procedure code (CPT): 23472

After review, this request is DENIED. Reason for determination: the documentation submitted was incomplete and does not allow a determination of medical necessity.

This determination was made under the plan's applicable medical policy and clinical review criteria. You have the right to appeal this decision. Your appeal must be received within 180 days of the date of this notice (by 2027-01-31).

Reference number: POC-9AB63CFCDF-18778


---

4. State the appeal deadline.

the patient can obtain the criteria that were applied to them.

The current published literature on this topic only includes short -term follow- ups, and many studies are small in scale, non-randomized, or lack control groups. Additionally, there is considerable variability in study design, which makes direct comparisons to other treatments challenging. Another significant concern is that many of these studies are industry-sponsored or authored by device developers, which introduces potential bias into the findings. Further high-quality studies are needed to address these limitations. The InSpace™ Subacromial Tissue Spacer System (Stryker) is a minimally invasive, biodegradable balloon spacer for treating massive, inoperable rotator cuff tears (MIRCTs). According to the manufacturer, it preserves musculoskeletal and bone tissues, does not require the use of an anchor, and does not require a permanent implant. It is used as a spacer to eliminate friction between the acromion and the humeral head or rotator cuff to restore shoulder function and reduce pain. It is designed to biodegrade over the course of twelve months. In 2025a, Hayes developed an Evolving Evidence Review focused on using the InSpace biodegradable subacromial spacer (Stryker) alone or with debridement for rotator cuff tears. After a review of full -text clinical studies and systematic Surgery of the Shoulder Page 3 of 6 UnitedHealthcare Commercial and Individual Exchange Medical Policy Effective 09/01/2026 Proprietary Information of UnitedHealthcare. Copyright 2026 United HealthCare Services, Inc. reviews, it was found that there is minimal support for using the InSpace biodegradable subacromial spacer alone or with debridement for treating massive irreparable rotator cuff tears. Furthermore, a review of practice guidelines and position statements determined that there is no/unclear support for using the technology alone or with debridement for treating massive irreparable rotator cuff tears regardless of whether spacers were used alone, with debridement, or as an adjunct to partial rotator cuff repair. In a 2025b, Evolving Evidence Review by Hayes, the InSpace biodegradable subacromial spacer (Stryker) was evaluated as an adjunct to partial repair of rotator cuff tears. After reviewing full-text clinical studies, and systematic reviews, it was found that there is minimal support for using the InSpace biodegradable subacromial spacer as an adjunct to partial repair for treating massive irreparable rotator cuff tears. Additionally, after reviewing full-text clinical practice guidelines and position statements, it was determined that there is no/unclear support for using biodegradable subacromial spacers for treating massive irreparable rotator cuff tears, regardless of whether spacers were utilized as an alternative or an adjunct to partial rotator cuff repair. Sandler and associates (2024) conducted a dual-armed systematic review and meta-analysis of over 1000 individuals to compare the outcomes after SAB spacer placement versus arthroscopic debridement for MIRCTs. For the SAB arm, 14 of 449 studies were considered eligible for inclusion, while 14 of 272 were considered eligible for inclusion in the debridement arm. In total 528 individuals eligible for inclusion in the SAB arm, 479 in the debridement arm, and 69.9% of those individuals undergoing SAB placement also underwent concomitant debridement. The findings include decreases in the visual analog scale (VAS) pain score and increases in the Constant score were found to be significantly more following debridement [–0.7 points (p < 0.001) and ±5.5 points (p < 0.001), respectively], although the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) for the VAS was not attained after either procedure. Both SAB placement and debridement significantly improved the range of motion (ROM) in forward flexion/forward elevation, internal and external rotation, and abduction (p < 0.001). Rates of general complication were greater following debridement versus SAB placement (5.2% ±5.6% vs. 3.5% ±6.3%, respectively; p < 0.001); however, there were no significant variances among SAB placement and debridement in rates of persistent symptoms necessitating a reintervention (3.3% ±6.2% vs 3.8% ±7.3%, respectively; p = 0.252) or reoperation rates (5.1% ±7.6% vs 4.8% ±8.4%, respectively; p = 0.552). The mean time to conversion to reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (RTSA) was 11.0 versus 25.4 months, respectively, for the SAB versus debridement arm. The limitations of the analysis include inconsistencies between follow-up times, with the follow-up time associated with debridement being nearly twice as long as the follow-up time related to SAB placement, are likely attributable to the recentness of SAB use globally, which may confuse evaluations with older debridement literature given the evolution in arthroscopic surgery over time. The time to reverse total shoulder arthroplasty was not uniformly reported between studies and was decided based on either individual patient data or weighted means. Also, there was heterogeneity in using and reporting rotator cuff tears size and type, further obscuring direct comparisons. The authors concluded that while SAB placement was associated with adequate postoperative outcomes for treating MIRCTs, there was no clear advantage over debridement only. Shorter operative times combined with better postoperative results and prolonged times to conversion to reverse total shoulder arthroplasty supported debridement as a more desirable choice. While there may be a role for SAB placement in poor surgical candidates, there is promising evidence to support debridement alone with no SAB placement for treating MIRCTs (Level IV evidence).
